name: Czechia
summary_text: Czechia no longer conditions official legal gender change on surgery including sterilisation. On 24 April 2024 the Czech Constitutional Court in judgment PL. US 52/23 held that making recognition conditional on disabling reproductive function was unconstitutional.  Reuters reported in June 2025 that the surgery requirement had been dropped. In July 2025 the Czech Health Ministry announced that trans people would no longer be required to undergo surgery or hormone treatment to change legal gender. On 12 September 2025 the European Court of Human Rights in T.H. v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 33037/22) found a violation of Article 8 in the surgical and sterilisation condition and related civil registry treatment, with Transgender Europe and ILGA-Europe intervening, and framed Convention-guaranteed recognition through self-determination.  Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised. It was decriminalised in 1962. Homosexual prostitution was decriminalised and the age of consent was equalised at 15 in 1990.  The 2009 Anti-Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, housing and access to goods and services.  Police recorded 94 hate crimes in 2024, with 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced, a series that includes LGBTI motivation in the bias breakdown. The Criminal Code has moved from a hostility model to a discriminatory-selection model. ODIHR observed that recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes. The government approved an amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, which remained pending in Parliament, while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened particularly vulnerable victim status.  Detained trans foreigners have supreme-court level placement safeguards but practice is inconsistent. On 20 March 2023 reporting described a clash between administrative courts over immigration police handling of a detained HIV-positive trans man in transition. The Supreme Administrative Court rebuked sarcastic moral lectures from the Prague Municipal Court and required authorities to assess first whether detainees are potentially vulnerable persons before placement.  Prison placement is a documented and unresolved risk. Reporting on 18 November 2025 found Czech prisons unprepared for trans people and without clear rules. The Supreme Court requires the national prison concept to address explicitly the needs of people in or after transition in light of the Constitutional Court ruling. The human-rights commissioner seeks a binding regulation while the Justice Ministry maintains the existing framework suffices, with consultation ongoing.  Partner recognition is substantial but stops short of full marriage equality. Since 2001 persons living in a common household have held hospital and prison visitation rights as well as inheritance and housing succession rights. Registered partnership for same-sex couples took effect on 1 July 2006 after a presidential veto was overturned. A 2024 compromise law placed same-sex partnerships in the civil code on terms equated to marriage in all aspects except joint adoption while permitting step-child adoption, effective 1 January 2025.  Official rhetoric toward trans people has been hostile. On 27 June 2021 President Milos Zeman said sex-reassignment surgery meant committing a crime through self-harm and said trans people disgusted him. After the Constitutional Court repeal, the Justice Minister said his goal was to prevent men from giving birth, other politicians issued transphobic statements, and the far-right SPD circulated election leaflets promising to take money from LGBT activists and give more to families. In survey data, reported exposure to anti-LGBT speech by politicians rose from 43 percent in 2018 to 71 percent in 2023, with 63 percent attributing rising intolerance to politicians.  Survey and incident data show elevated risk for trans and non-binary people. A Being LGBTQ+ in Czechia survey found 43 percent had experienced discrimination or harassment in the past five years, over a third within the prior 12 months, highest among trans and non-binary respondents, and 51 percent had been targeted by insults, assault or threats in five years. In June 2023 a group disrupted a Brno Pride drag story-time event with homophobic slurs.  Prague and Brno were rated highest for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, with formal nondiscrimination policies, queer districts in Vinohrady and Zizkov, and hostels offering concierge support, private rooms and organised socials. Harassment risk was reported to concentrate in rural areas and late-night settings.  The new Asylum Law includes sexual orientation and gender identity grounds and provides an opposite-gender interview option.

Survey and incident data show elevated risk for trans and non-binary people. A Being LGBTQ+ in Czechia survey found 43 percent had experienced discrimination or harassment in the past five years, over a third within the prior 12 months, highest among trans and non-binary respondents, and 51 percent had been targeted by insults, assault or threats in five years. In June 2023 a group disrupted a Brno Pride drag story-time event with homophobic slurs.  Prague and Brno were rated highest for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, with formal nondiscrimination policies, queer districts in Vinohrady and Zizkov, and hostels offering concierge support, private rooms and organised socials. Harassment risk was reported to concentrate in rural areas and late-night settings.  The new Asylum Law includes sexual orientation and gender identity grounds and provides an opposite-gender interview option.
